Executive 'rber.
Mr. William H. H. Bowen may be reinstated in the field service of
the Internal Revenue Service without regard to the year limit required by
the civil service rules.
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the
Treasury with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. The
Secretary of the Treasury states that Mr. Bowen served very efficiently in
the Internal Revenue Service for nineteen years and resigned from the
position of internal revenue agent to accept the appointment of postmaster
at Covington, Kentucky, retiring from that position on September 1, 1914;
that the records of the Department show that the work performed by
Mr. Bowen as internal revenue agent wvas of an unusually efficient char-
acter; and the Internal Revenue Service at this time is in need of such
men as Mr. Bowen, men who are able to take up successfully any and
every phase of the internal revenue work. Mr. Bowen, acting on infor-
mation inadvertently given by a Commissioner, failed to make application
for reinstatement in the Internal Revenue Service before the expiration of
the year limit, required by the rules.
WOODROW WILSON
THE WHITE HOUSE,
;,r4 October, 1915.
[No. 2258.]

Mr. Charles Hardin may be reinstated as a clerk at not to exceed
$1200 per annum in the Post Office Department without regard to the
length of his separation from the service.

examination as a clerk at $900 in the Post Office Department at Washing-
ton, and was removed from the position of clerk class 3 ($i6oo) on January
26, I901, for irregularities in connection with the dead letter sale. The

believed that the removal of Mr. Hardin, and the manner by which he

Miss Emma I. Windridge, who has passed the civil service examina-
tion in stenography and typewriting, may be appointed to a clerkship in
the War Department without reference to the civil service rules.
Miss Windridge is the daughter of Charles E. Windridge, formerly a
clerk in the War Department. Her father was appointed to a position in

expected_title: Executive Order 2285—Requiring American Citizens Traveling Abroad to Procure Passports

machine_read.first_words: All persons leaving the United States for foreign countries should be provided
machine_read.last_words: necessary for that purpose WOO DROW WILSONl THE WHITE HOUSE December NO

head:
Executive Orber
All persons leaving the United States for foreign countries should be
provided with passports of the Governments of which they are citizens.
These documents are rendered necessary because the regulations of all
European countries and of several other foreign countries require pass-
ports or other documents of identification of all persons who enter their
boundaries. The Secretary of State, in cooperation with the Secretary of
the Treasury, will make arrangements for the inspection of passports of all
persons, American or foreign, leaving this country, and the fact that these
passports have been seen will be stamped thereon.
All applications to the Secretary of State for passports from Ameri-
can citizens must be made in duplicate, and must be accompanied with
three copies of the photograph of the applicant. Each applicant for a
passport must inform the Department of State at what point he intends to
depart, on what date, and by what ship if he sails from an American port.
Applications shall be made in the manner heretofore prescribed by
the rules governing the granting and issuing of passports, but the Secre-
tary of State may designate an agent or agents to take applications, and
wherever his agent is stationed applications shall be made only before him.
This Order wvill become effective as soon as the Secretary of State
and Secretary of the Treasury have made the arrangements necessary for
that purpose.
WOO DROW WILSONl
THE WHITE HOUSE,
15 December, 1Q15.

head:
Executive ether.
Miss Margaret S. Neate may be appointed a printer's assistant in the
Bureau of Engraving and Printing without certification by the Civil
Service Commission.
Miss Neate passed the examination for printer's assistant in January,
1915, but has not been reached for certification. She is the daughter of
Dr. John S. Neate, who served for twenty-two years in the United States
Army, and rendered most valuable service in fighting yellow fever, sub-
mitting himself for experiment, and died in 1912 from a disease believed
to have been brought on by this service.
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the
Treasury. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recoin-
mend at ion.
WOODROW WILSON
THE WHITE HousE,
7 February, 1916.
[No. 2306.]
